Senses.Explanation: A barren woman, literally a “stone woman,” is a stock figure assigned impossible actions. Weilin has her return at dawn wearing a hat, and Fushan says that a stone woman by a cliff sees through a claim. Baiyu Jingsi makes the biological floor explicit by comparing an imposed sermon to forcing a stone woman to bear a child; Shu’an Fancong says she has no husband. A lamp recension preserves Dongshan Liangjie’s historically important pairing of a wooden man singing with a stone woman dancing. The image is impossible by design, but the sources do not turn it into a separate doctrine.

Hongzhi and Guting quote the child in restraints; Juelang says the teaching milk nurses it; Yongji pairs it with a wooden puppet and impossible seasons; Huigong asks what sort of clever figure this barren woman’s child is; Tianran places it beside rabbit horns, turtle hair, and a pregnant pillar; and Zhanran promises an answer when the child gives birth. Senses.Note: A stone woman cannot bear a child; that impossibility is why the line can interrupt a predictable answer. Huiyue offers it as his own answer to what happens when the year ends and then makes a new verse from it. Juelang places the birth at Huangmei in a verse to a patron. Huigong quotes Furong earlier line and asks where the child could put its feet, refusing to leave the image as an easy marvel. Baiyu calls it news carried from another region. Biemu speaks it after declaring a seven-day session complete. Each use makes the impossible event press on a particular listener or occasion.

Senses.Note: Dongshan verse places a dancing stone woman beside a singing wooden man, making activity appear where ordinary expectation allows none. Liangting speaks the pair while explaining continuity that is not assembled by conscious calculation. Azi warns that repeating the stone woman and other impossible marvels can still leave a listener dark inside. Yongjue reads Dongshan line as a way to describe spontaneous use beyond clever effort. Weilin speaks it while addressing the reprinting of a scripture commentary. The image can open a question, but merely owning its strange words is not the answer.

Senses.Explanation: The utmost way is not difficult opens Sengcan’s Inscription on Trusting Mind and immediately pairs that claim with “it only rejects choosing.” Zen records do not preserve it as a soothing maxim. Zhaozhou makes it a public question about choosing, speech, and clarity, while Yongjue Yuanxian refuses both difficult and easy. The formula is a recurring test of anyone who tries to settle in either side.

Senses.Explanation: The supreme Way is not difficult; it only dislikes choosing and rejecting. The inherited line turns attention from preference-making toward unforced accord. Senses.Note: The Xinxin Ming opens by saying that the highest way is not difficult; the trouble lies in picking and rejecting. Hansong, Zhuanyu, and Yongjue quote the traditionally attributed verse and ask what that warning means in a present encounter. Binya, Shitian, and Tianyin voice the pair directly in their own sermons, often pointing to ordinary distinctions and asking where choice begins. The next verse line turns to love and aversion, but the opening pair also recurs as a complete question in these records.
